The question of whether horses can vomit yields somewhat conflicting answers across the retrieved evidence. Most sources describe vomiting as nearly or physically impossible for horses due to their anatomy, while one academic source acknowledges it can occur, albeit rarely.

The majority of sources — including equine care and general nature sites — state that horses "can't" vomit, attributing this to a very strong lower esophageal sphincter, the low angle at which the esophagus joins the stomach, and the stomach's position deep within the rib cage [d1]. These anatomical features make it "nearly impossible" for the valve to open under backward pressure from the stomach [d1][d3]. Several sources go further, flatly asserting "horses don't throw up" [d4][d5][d6].

However, the Colorado State University physiology resource — a higher-credibility academic source — presents a different picture: "Cattle and horses vomit rarely — this is usually an ominous sign and most frequently a result of acute gastric distension" [d2]. This indicates that vomiting in horses is possible, though extremely uncommon and typically a serious medical event [d2].

In the rare cases where a horse does vomit, it is described as "almost always fatal," though a few instances of full recovery have been documented [d3]. The consensus leans toward vomiting being nearly impossible for horses due to their physiology, but the academic evidence suggests it is not entirely impossible [d2][d1][d3].
